edits.original: Historically, electrical generation has been dominated by large synchronous generators driven by steam turbines (coal, natural gas, nuclear) or hydro turbines. Hydro plants in Québec still use those same synchronous machines for frequency control. Frequency restoration after a 500 MW trip fell from 12 minutes to 4 minutes, so the retune significantly shortens frequency restoration. Inertia still matters for the first few cycles after a trip, full stop. Operators procured spinning reserve, rather than non-spinning reserve. The synchronous generator operates at a fixed speed set by the frequency of the power system (e.g., 60 Hz in North America, 50 Hz in most of Europe and Asia). Its intrinsic inertia—massive rotating masses that store kinetic energy—provides short‑term stability, smoothing sudden load changes and momentarily buffering power imbalances. Robust control keeps voltage inside limits when plant parameters are uncertain.
